newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: JABILUKA MINE EIS DUE TODAY
The company bidding to develop a uranium mine on the edge of Kakadu National Park says the mine will not damage the park's World Heritage values.
The Environmental Impact Statement for the proposed Jabiluka uranium mine, in the Northern Territory, is expected to be handed to the Federal Government today.
Energy Resources of Australia says the successful operation of its existing Ranger uranium mine inside Kakadu proves it can carry on uranium mining in the area without adverse environmental impact.
ERA says the two mines could yield Australia $12 billion during the next 30 years.
Company chief, Phillip Shirvington, says the final E-I-S addresses concerns such as water management, which he says have been successfully handled at Ranger over 16 years.
There is also detail in the statement about estimated radiation levels, and the possible social impact on local Aborigines.
Despite the company's optimism, the area's traditional owners continue to oppose the mine.
They have lodged a Federal Court application aimed at stopping it.
TOURISM INDUSTRY ACCUSED OF NOT PLANNING FOR FUTURE
The tourism industry has been accused of failing to nuture the Japanese tourist market.
Qantas Japan General Manager, Col Hughes' comments follow the announcement that a $10 million promotional campaign will kick-off in Japan in January.
The campaign aims to halt the slowdown in growth of the number of Japanese visitor to Australia.
Mr Hughes says the Japan market had made a lot of money for Australia, but nobody had been looking to the future.
He says not enough people in the industry thought about what to do if growth did slow.
ANTI-HANSON AND PRO-HANSON CROWDS GATHER IN VIC
The launch of Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party in Horsham, in country Victoria, last night, drew a crowd of about 300 enthusiastic supporters.
The party's Victorian branch co-ordinator, Andrew Carne, told the crowd about the need to restrict foreign ownership, restore tariff protection and cut back immigration.
Mr Carne described the response as fantastic, saying interaction with the crowd after his speech underlined the views of the party's supporters.
Meanwhile, about two blocks away, around 140 people gathered at the town's Masonic Hall for a peaceful protest against the views of One Nation.

Demonstration organiser, Gayle Crook, says she decided to organise a peaceful protest, because rowdy scenes which have taken place in other cities and towns around Australia have been counter-productive.
TAXPACKS TO BE DELIVERED FROM TODAY
The Australian Tax Office begins deliveries of this year's Taxpack to rural areas today, with metropolitan areas to follow. Last year, 3,000,000 people used the Taxpack to lodge their own tax return.
Tax changes introduced by the Federal Government this year include the family tax assistance, where taxpayers with dependent children can claim a higher tax-free threshold if they meet income tests.
The Taxpack also includes for the first time a short tax form, just four pages, compared with the standard eight pages.
But the Tax and Accountants' Association says the Taxpack should have included the actual questions that might be asked in an audit.
President Ray Regan says last year, the Commissioner of Taxation audited some 235,000 taxpayers, with 70 per cent having to pay back a total of $67 million dollars.
COALITION MPS TO GAUGE COMMUNITY SUPPORT FOR TAX REFORM
Last night's special meeting on tax reform has seen Coalition MPs told to gauge community support for reform, and report back to the Government.
The Treasurer, Peter Costello, says the meeting expressed strong support for change.

Liberal, Ross Cameron, says while his survey of voters in his Parramatta electorate found strong support for a Goods and Services Tax, some MPs think a GST is politically risky, with the lessons of 1993 weighing on people's minds.
But Mr Costello says the community knows the tax system leaves a lot to be desired, and that it has to be improved for the sake of exports and jobs.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
